GI-1.t: Identify the foregut, midgut, and hindgut derivatives and their arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric), and explain why visceral pain from each is referred to the epigastric, periumbilical, or suprapubic region.

Describe physiologic herniation of the midgut in week 6, its 270 degree counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery, and its return by week 10, and predict the results of malrotation and of failed return (omphalocele).
GI-1.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Congenital disorders: malrotation; abdominal wall defects

GI-1.t: Explain how the tracheoesophageal septum divides the foregut into the esophagus and the respiratory diverticulum, and relate incomplete division to esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula.
GI-1.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Congenital disorders: esophageal atresia; tracheoesophageal fistula

GI-1.t: Describe development of the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts from the hepatic diverticulum and of the pancreas from dorsal and ventral buds, and relate abnormal ventral bud migration to annular pancreas and failed duct fusion to pancreas divisum.
Explain how neural crest cells migrate to form the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, and relate failed migration (RET mutations) to the aganglionic distal segment of Hirschsprung disease.
Describe recanalization of the duodenal lumen and relate its failure to duodenal atresia, with bilious vomiting, the double bubble sign, and an association with Down syndrome.

GI-2.t: Identify the four layers of the gastrointestinal wall (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa or adventitia) and locate the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses within them.

Compare the epithelium of the esophagus (nonkeratinized stratified squamous), stomach and intestine (simple columnar), and anal canal (columnar above the pectinate line, stratified squamous below), and relate the gastroesophageal junction to Barrett metaplasia.

Identify gastric parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor), chief cells (pepsinogen), mucous neck cells, and antral G cells (gastrin), and predict which secretions fall when autoimmune gastritis destroys the body and fundus mucosa.
GI-2.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastritis

GI-2.t: Distinguish the duodenum (Brunner glands in the submucosa), jejunum (tall plicae circulares), ileum (Peyer patches), and colon (crypts rich in goblet cells, no villi) on histologic sections.

Describe the hepatic lobule and acinus, including the portal triad, sinusoids, space of Disse, Kupffer cells, and stellate (Ito) cells, and explain why zone 3 is most vulnerable to ischemia and to acetaminophen injury.
GI-2.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: noninfectious hepatitis

GI-2.t: Distinguish pancreatic acini with zymogen granules from islets of Langerhans, and compare serous and mucous salivary acini, identifying the parotid as a mainly serous gland.

GI-3.t: Identify the parts of the stomach (cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus) and the four parts of the duodenum, and locate the major duodenal papilla in the second part.

Classify abdominal organs as intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal, naming the retroperitoneal gut structures (duodenum parts 2 to 4, pancreas except the tail, ascending and descending colon, and part of the rectum).

Describe the liver lobes, bare area, and porta hepatis, and trace bile from the hepatic ducts to the common bile duct, which joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater under the sphincter of Oddi.
Distinguish the colon from the small intestine by taeniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices, and locate the base of the appendix at McBurney point where the taeniae converge.

Locate the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands and their ducts, including the parotid duct opening opposite the upper second molar, and explain why parotid disease can involve the facial nerve passing through the gland.

GI-4.t: Trace the esophagus from the pharynx through the superior and posterior mediastinum to the stomach, naming its three narrowings: the cricopharyngeus, the crossing of the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10.

Relate the innervation of the tongue (CN V3 and CN VII to the anterior two thirds, CN IX to the posterior third, CN XII motor except palatoglossus by CN X) to the deficit produced by a given nerve lesion.

Describe the greater and lesser sacs, the greater and lesser omentum, and the omental (epiploic) foramen, and identify the hepatoduodenal ligament contents (portal vein, proper hepatic artery, common bile duct).

Identify the structures carried by the falciform (ligamentum teres), gastrohepatic (gastric arteries), gastrosplenic (short gastric vessels), and splenorenal (splenic artery and vein, pancreatic tail) ligaments.

Describe the boundaries of the inguinal canal and Hesselbach triangle, and distinguish indirect (lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, through the deep ring), direct (medial, through the triangle), and femoral (below the inguinal ligament) hernias.
GI-4.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: inguinal, femoral, and abdominal wall hernias

GI-4.t: Locate the dependent peritoneal spaces where fluid, pus, or blood collects (hepatorenal pouch of Morison when supine, rectouterine or rectovesical pouch when upright, subphrenic spaces) and relate them to abscess formation.
GI-4.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatic, subhepatic, and subphrenic abscess

GI-5.t: Trace the branches of the celiac trunk (left gastric, splenic, common hepatic) to the stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, and duodenum, and identify the gastroduodenal artery as the vessel eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer.
GI-5.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: peptic ulcer

GI-5.t: Describe the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and the marginal artery, and predict ischemic colitis at the watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction) after hypotension.
GI-5.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: mesenteric ischemia, ischemic colitis

GI-5.t: Trace portal blood from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, which join behind the pancreatic neck, through the liver sinusoids and central veins to the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava.

Identify the portosystemic anastomoses (left gastric to esophageal veins draining to azygos, paraumbilical to abdominal wall veins, superior to middle and inferior rectal veins) and predict varices and caput medusae in portal hypertension.
GI-5.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: portal hypertension, esophageal varices

GI-5.t: Compare the anal canal above and below the pectinate line by epithelium, arterial supply, venous drainage (portal versus systemic), lymph drainage (internal iliac versus superficial inguinal), and pain sensation (visceral versus somatic).
GI-5.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: hemorrhoids

GI-5.t: Explain the dual blood supply of the liver (most flow from the portal vein, the rest from the hepatic artery) and why hepatic infarction is uncommon while the bile ducts depend on hepatic arterial flow.

GI-6.t: Describe mastication by the muscles of mastication (CN V3), the voluntary oral and reflex pharyngeal and esophageal phases of swallowing coordinated by the medulla, and vagal nitric oxide and VIP relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and proximal stomach.

Explain how slow waves from the interstitial cells of Cajal set contraction frequency, how the myenteric plexus coordinates peristalsis (contraction above and relaxation below a bolus), and how motilin drives the fasting migrating motor complex.

Explain the cephalic, gastric, and intestinal phases of gastric acid secretion, including parietal cell stimulation by acetylcholine, gastrin, and histamine, inhibition by somatostatin, and the H+/K+ ATPase as the final step.
Relate gastrin, cholecystokinin, secretin, GIP, and motilin to their source cells (G, I, S, K, M) and stimuli, and predict the hormonal response to a meal that delivers acid and fat to the duodenum.

Explain carbohydrate, protein, and fat digestion by salivary and pancreatic amylase, brush border disaccharidases, enteropeptidase activation of trypsinogen, and pancreatic lipase acting with bile salts.

Describe the defecation reflex (rectal distension, reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter, voluntary control of the external sphincter by the pudendal nerve) and the gastrocolic reflex, and predict incontinence from loss of each element.
GI-6.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: fecal incontinence

GI-6.t: Explain how vomiting is triggered through the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema and the medullary vomiting center, and predict the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis of prolonged vomiting.
GI-6.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Signs, symptoms, and ill-defined disorders: nausea, vomiting

GI-7.t: Explain monosaccharide absorption (SGLT1 sodium cotransport of glucose and galactose, GLUT5 uptake of fructose, GLUT2 basolateral exit) and why glucose plus sodium in oral rehydration solution increases water absorption.

Explain absorption of free amino acids by sodium-linked transporters and of dipeptides and tripeptides by H+ cotransport (PepT1), and relate the neutral amino acid transport defect of Hartnup disease to pellagra-like findings.

Trace fat absorption from micelles to re-esterification in enterocytes, packaging with apoB-48 into chylomicrons, and entry into lacteals, and predict steatorrhea, acanthocytes, and vitamin E deficiency in abetalipoproteinemia.
Identify where iron (duodenum), folate (jejunum), and vitamin B12 and bile acids (terminal ileum) are absorbed, and predict the deficiencies that follow duodenal disease or ileal resection.
GI-7.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: malnutrition and malabsorption, short bowel syndrome

GI-7.t: Explain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids with active reabsorption in the terminal ileum, and predict steatorrhea and cholesterol gallstone risk when ileal disease or resection interrupts it.

Compare secretory diarrhea (cholera toxin raising cAMP and opening CFTR chloride channels), osmotic diarrhea (unabsorbed lactose), and inflammatory diarrhea, and use the stool osmotic gap and response to fasting to distinguish them.
GI-7.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Signs, symptoms, and ill-defined disorders: diarrhea

GI-8.t: Identify the essential amino acids and essential fatty acids (linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid) required in the diet, and compare kwashiorkor (protein deficiency, edema from hypoalbuminemia, fatty liver) with marasmus (calorie deficiency, wasting without edema).

Explain how fat malabsorption (pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, celiac disease) causes deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K, and predict night blindness, osteomalacia, hemolytic anemia with neuropathy, and a prolonged PT.

Trace vitamin B12 absorption (release by acid and pepsin, haptocorrin binding, pancreatic protease cleavage, intrinsic factor binding, ileal uptake) and distinguish B12 from folate deficiency by methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels.
GI-8.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin B9 and B12 deficiency

GI-8.t: Relate deficiencies of thiamine (Wernicke encephalopathy, beriberi), niacin (pellagra), pyridoxine (sideroblastic anemia, seizures), and vitamin C (scurvy from impaired collagen hydroxylation) to the cofactor role of each vitamin.
GI-8.usmle: Multisystem: Nutrition: vitamin B1, B3, B6, and C deficiency

GI-8.t: Explain endogenous energy production in the fed and fasting states, including hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis from alanine, lactate, and glycerol, and hepatic ketogenesis, and why the liver cannot use the ketones it makes.

Relate deficiencies of minerals absorbed in the gut to their findings: iron (microcytic anemia), zinc (poor wound healing, dysgeusia, acrodermatitis), and copper (anemia, neutropenia, myelopathy), including copper deficiency from excess zinc or gastric bypass.
Predict the findings of vitamin A toxicity (intracranial hypertension, liver injury, teratogenicity) and vitamin D toxicity (hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, kidney stones).

GI-9.t: Trace bilirubin from heme breakdown (heme oxygenase, biliverdin reductase) through albumin transport, hepatic conjugation by UGT1A1, canalicular excretion by MRP2, and conversion by gut bacteria to urobilinogen and stercobilin.
GI-9.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: jaundice

GI-9.t: Interpret conjugated and unconjugated serum bilirubin, urine bilirubin, and urine urobilinogen to distinguish hemolytic, hepatocellular, and obstructive jaundice.
GI-9.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: jaundice

GI-9.t: Explain phase I (cytochrome P450) and phase II (glucuronidation, sulfation, glutathione conjugation) biotransformation, and use acetaminophen overdose to show how glutathione depletion lets NAPQI cause zone 3 necrosis.
GI-9.usmle: Multisystem: Toxins and environmental injury: acetaminophen

GI-9.t: Explain carbon tetrachloride hepatotoxicity as cytochrome P450 conversion to the trichloromethyl free radical, which causes lipid peroxidation, fatty change, and centrilobular necrosis.
GI-9.usmle: Multisystem: Toxins and environmental injury: carbon tetrachloride

GI-9.t: Explain the synthetic and metabolic functions of the liver (albumin, clotting factors, urea cycle disposal of ammonia), and predict hypoalbuminemia, a prolonged PT, and hyperammonemia in liver failure.
GI-9.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: end-stage liver disease

GI-9.t: Describe the protective functions of saliva (bicarbonate buffering, IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin, enamel remineralization) and predict dental caries when salivary flow falls.
GI-9.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: dental caries

GI-9.t: Explain how the gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing sodium and water and contracts under cholecystokinin, and relate stasis and concentration to gallstone formation.

GI-10.t: Explain hereditary hemochromatosis (autosomal recessive HFE C282Y mutation, inappropriately low hepcidin, excess iron absorption) and predict cirrhosis, diabetes, skin bronzing, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, and hepatocellular carcinoma risk.
GI-10.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: hemochromatosis

GI-10.t: Explain Wilson disease (autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation, failed biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading) and relate it to low serum ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, basal ganglia degeneration, and hepatitis or cirrhosis.
GI-10.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: Wilson disease

GI-10.t: Explain how the PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin variant misfolds and is retained in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules causing cirrhosis, while low serum levels cause panacinar emphysema.
GI-10.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

GI-10.t: Compare the adenoma to carcinoma sequence (APC loss, KRAS activation, TP53 loss) with the mismatch repair pathway (MLH1, MSH2, microsatellite instability) of Lynch syndrome in colorectal cancer.
GI-10.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: hereditary colon cancer syndromes

GI-10.t: Distinguish familial adenomatous polyposis (autosomal dominant APC, hundreds of adenomas), Gardner and Turcot variants, MUTYH-associated polyposis (autosomal recessive), and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11, hamartomas, mucocutaneous pigmentation).
GI-10.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: hereditary colon cancer syndromes; MUTYH-associated polyposis

GI-10.t: Relate CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis to meconium ileus, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and focal biliary cirrhosis.
GI-10.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic, metabolic, and developmental disorders: cystic fibrosis

GI-11.t: Describe mucosal immunity in the gut, including antigen sampling by M cells over Peyer patches, secretory IgA transported by the polymeric Ig receptor, and oral tolerance, and relate selective IgA deficiency to recurrent mucosal infections.

Explain celiac disease immunopathogenesis: tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin, HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 presents it to CD4 T cells, and IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies appear.
GI-11.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: celiac disease

GI-11.t: Explain how NOD2 variants, impaired handling of commensal bacteria, and Th1 and Th17 responses produce transmural granulomatous inflammation in Crohn disease.
GI-11.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: inflammatory bowel disease

GI-11.t: Match autoimmune gastrointestinal diseases to their autoantibodies: autoimmune gastritis (parietal cell and intrinsic factor), autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-LKM1), and primary biliary cholangitis (antimitochondrial).
GI-11.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: autoimmune hepatitis

GI-11.t: Explain how chronic Helicobacter pylori antigen stimulation drives B cell proliferation in gastric MALT lymphoma, and why early lesions can regress when the organism is eradicated.

Explain that hepatocyte injury in hepatitis B is caused mainly by cytotoxic CD8 T cells rather than the virus itself, and relate HBsAg immune complexes to polyarteritis nodosa and membranous nephropathy.
GI-11.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatitis B

GI-11.t: Explain why hepatitis B vaccination with recombinant HBsAg produces anti-HBs without anti-HBc, so serology separates vaccine immunity from resolved infection.
GI-11.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatitis B

GI-12.t: Distinguish toxin-mediated causes of diarrhea and vomiting: preformed Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus toxins (onset within hours), cholera toxin and the ETEC heat-labile toxin (both raise cAMP), and Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B.
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: enteric infections

GI-12.t: Compare invasive enteric bacteria by key features: Shigella (nonmotile, very low infectious dose), Salmonella (motile, H2S producing), and Campylobacter jejuni (comma-shaped, grows at 42 degrees C (107.6 degrees F), poultry).
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter

GI-12.t: Describe Yersinia enterocolitica (mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis), EHEC O157:H7 (Shiga toxin, bloody diarrhea, hemolytic uremic syndrome), and Listeria monocytogenes (deli meats and soft cheese, actin-based cell-to-cell spread).
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: Yersinia, E. coli, Listeria

GI-12.t: Compare the viral causes of enteritis: rotavirus (segmented dsRNA, villus damage in infants), norovirus (ssRNA calicivirus, outbreaks), and the enteroviruses coxsackievirus and echovirus (ssRNA picornaviruses, fecal-oral).
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: rotavirus, coxsackievirus, echovirus enteritis

GI-12.t: Compare hepatitis viruses: HAV (picornavirus, fecal-oral), HBV (partially dsDNA hepadnavirus with reverse transcriptase), HCV (flavivirus, high antigenic variation), HDV (defective, requires HBsAg), and HEV (fecal-oral, severe in pregnancy).
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatitis A, B, C, D, E

GI-12.t: Describe Helicobacter pylori as a curved, flagellated, microaerophilic gram-negative rod whose urease makes ammonia to buffer acid, and identify the urea breath test, stool antigen, and biopsy as ways to detect it.
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastritis, peptic ulcer

GI-12.t: Compare intestinal parasites: Giardia (cysts in water, fatty diarrhea), Entamoeba histolytica (flask-shaped ulcers, liver abscess), Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and Cystoisospora (acid-fast oocysts), and Strongyloides (skin-penetrating larvae, autoinfection, hyperinfection with corticosteroids).
GI-12.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: parasitic infections

GI-13-A.t: Distinguish mumps parotitis (paramyxovirus, often bilateral, raised serum amylase, with orchitis, pancreatitis, or aseptic meningitis) from acute bacterial parotitis (Staphylococcus aureus, dehydrated or postoperative patients, pus at the parotid duct).
GI-13-A.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: mumps; Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: parotitis

GI-13-A.t: Explain why salivary stones form most often in the submandibular gland (more viscous saliva, upward duct course), and predict painful swelling with meals and secondary sialadenitis.
GI-13-A.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: salivary gland stones, sialadenitis

GI-13-B.t: Explain acute pancreatitis as premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsin and other enzymes, and identify its causes, led by gallstones and alcohol, plus hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, ERCP, mumps, trauma, and drugs such as thiazides.
GI-13-B.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the pancreas: acute pancreatitis

GI-13-B.t: Interpret the findings of acute pancreatitis: epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase above three times normal, fat necrosis with calcium soap formation and hypocalcemia, and Cullen and Grey Turner signs of retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
GI-13-B.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the pancreas: acute pancreatitis

GI-13-B.t: Predict complications of acute pancreatitis, including pseudocyst (lined by granulation tissue, not epithelium), necrosis with infection or abscess, ARDS, DIC, and hypovolemic shock.
GI-13-B.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the pancreas: pancreatic cyst, pseudocyst

GI-13-B.t: Describe chronic pancreatitis (alcohol, cystic fibrosis, ductal obstruction, hereditary PRSS1 and SPINK1 mutations) with fibrosis and calcifications, and predict exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency) and diabetes.
GI-13-B.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the pancreas: chronic and hereditary pancreatitis; pancreatic insufficiency

GI-13-C.t: Distinguish intrahepatic causes of cholestasis (drugs, pregnancy, total parenteral nutrition, primary biliary cholangitis) from extrahepatic obstruction, and interpret raised conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT, pruritus, pale stools, and xanthomas.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: bile duct obstruction, cholestasis

GI-13-C.t: Compare primary biliary cholangitis (middle-aged women, antimitochondrial antibody, granulomatous destruction of small intrahepatic ducts) with primary sclerosing cholangitis (ulcerative colitis, onion-skin fibrosis, beaded ducts, cholangiocarcinoma risk).
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: primary biliary cirrhosis; primary sclerosing cholangitis

GI-13-C.t: Explain how activated hepatic stellate cells lay down collagen in the space of Disse to produce bridging fibrosis and regenerative nodules in cirrhosis, and identify its main causes (alcohol, chronic HBV and HCV, fatty liver disease, metabolic disease).
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: cirrhosis

GI-13-C.t: Predict the findings of cirrhosis from hepatocellular failure (jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia, hyperestrogenism with spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, and hepatic encephalopathy with asterixis) and from portal hypertension.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: cirrhosis; hepatic encephalopathy; end-stage liver disease

GI-13-C.t: Explain hepatorenal syndrome (splanchnic vasodilation and renal vasoconstriction with histologically normal kidneys) and hepatopulmonary syndrome (intrapulmonary vascular dilation causing hypoxemia) as complications of cirrhosis.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: hepatorenal syndrome; hepatopulmonary syndrome

GI-13-C.t: Compare Gilbert syndrome (mildly reduced UGT1A1 activity, benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia during fasting, stress, or illness) with Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I (absent UGT1A1, kernicterus in infancy) and type II (partial deficiency, milder course).
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome

GI-13-C.t: Describe the progression of alcohol-related liver disease from steatosis to alcoholic hepatitis (hepatocyte ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophils) to cirrhosis, and interpret an AST to ALT ratio greater than 2.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: alcoholic fatty liver; noninfectious hepatitis

GI-13-C.t: Explain metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) as a result of insulin resistance and obesity, and distinguish simple steatosis from steatohepatitis (MASH) that can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: nonalcoholic fatty liver disease

GI-13-C.t: Distinguish autoimmune hepatitis (young women, hypergammaglobulinemia, interface hepatitis with plasma cells) from drug and toxin hepatitis, such as acetaminophen zone 3 necrosis and isoniazid hepatitis.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: autoimmune hepatitis; Gastrointestinal: Adverse effects of drugs: acetaminophen, isoniazid

GI-13-C.t: Classify causes of portal hypertension as prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis), or posthepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure), and predict ascites, splenomegaly, varices, and caput medusae.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: portal hypertension

GI-13-C.t: Distinguish Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2 defect, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, black pigmented liver) from Rotor syndrome (similar but milder, liver not pigmented) as benign inherited causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
GI-13-C.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: Dubin-Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome

GI-13-D.t: Explain acute calculous cholecystitis from persistent cystic duct obstruction with chemical then bacterial inflammation, interpret right upper quadrant pain, fever, Murphy sign, and leukocytosis, and contrast acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill patients.
GI-13-D.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: cholelithiasis, cholecystitis

GI-13-D.t: Identify chronic cholecystitis with a calcified porcelain gallbladder as a risk for gallbladder adenocarcinoma.

Compare cholesterol stones (bile supersaturated with cholesterol, gallbladder stasis; risks include female sex, obesity, pregnancy, estrogen, rapid weight loss) with black pigment stones (hemolysis) and brown pigment stones (biliary infection).
GI-13-D.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: cholelithiasis

GI-13-D.t: Predict the consequence of a gallstone by its location: biliary colic, choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice, ascending cholangitis (fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain), gallstone pancreatitis, and gallstone ileus through a cholecystoenteric fistula.
GI-13-D.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: choledocholithiasis; cholangitis; gallstone ileus

GI-13-D.t: Explain Mirizzi syndrome as a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct, producing obstructive jaundice.
GI-13-D.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: Mirizzi syndrome

GI-13-E.t: Explain the causes of achlorhydria (autoimmune atrophic gastritis, chronic H. pylori pangastritis, gastrectomy) and predict hypergastrinemia with ECL cell hyperplasia and carcinoid risk, impaired iron and B12 absorption, and bacterial overgrowth.
GI-13-E.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastritis

GI-13-E.t: Describe celiac disease findings: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytes mainly in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum, iron deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, and risk of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma.
GI-13-E.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: celiac disease

GI-13-E.t: Distinguish malabsorption from pancreatic enzyme deficiency (steatorrhea, low fecal elastase, normal D-xylose absorption) from mucosal disease (abnormal D-xylose absorption), and relate enteropeptidase deficiency to failed protease activation.
GI-13-E.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the pancreas: pancreatic insufficiency

GI-13-E.t: Explain how primary (adult-type) or secondary (after viral enteritis or celiac disease) lactase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhea, bloating, and flatulence after dairy, with a positive hydrogen breath test and normal villi in the primary form.
GI-13-E.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: lactose intolerance

GI-13-E.t: Predict the consequences of short bowel syndrome after extensive resection, including diarrhea, steatorrhea, B12 and bile acid loss after ileal resection, and calcium oxalate kidney stones from enteric hyperoxaluria.
GI-13-E.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: short bowel syndrome

GI-13-E.t: Explain how bacterial overgrowth in a blind loop after gastric surgery deconjugates bile acids and consumes vitamin B12, causing steatorrhea and B12 deficiency with normal or raised folate.
GI-13-E.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: post-gastric surgery syndromes (blind loop syndrome)

GI-13-F.t: Explain achalasia as loss of inhibitory (nitric oxide and VIP) neurons of the myenteric plexus, producing incomplete LES relaxation and aperistalsis, with dysphagia to solids and liquids, a bird-beak barium swallow, and Chagas disease as a secondary cause.
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: achalasia

GI-13-F.t: Distinguish adynamic (paralytic) ileus (after abdominal surgery, hypokalemia, peritonitis, opioids; absent bowel sounds, diffuse gas) from mechanical obstruction (adhesions, hernias, tumors, impaction; high-pitched bowel sounds, dilated loops proximal to a transition point).
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: paralytic ileus; intestinal obstruction

GI-13-F.t: Distinguish sliding from paraesophageal hiatal hernia, and explain how an incarcerated abdominal wall hernia becomes strangulated as venous congestion leads to arterial compromise and bowel infarction.
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: paraesophageal (hiatal) hernia; Gastrointestinal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: hernias

GI-13-F.t: Compare intussusception (telescoping, usually ileocolic in young children, a lead point such as hypertrophied Peyer patches or Meckel diverticulum, currant jelly stool) with volvulus (twisting on the mesentery, sigmoid in older adults, midgut with malrotation in infants).
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: intussusception; volvulus

GI-13-F.t: Distinguish causes of megacolon: Hirschsprung disease (absent ganglion cells in the rectum, delayed passage of meconium, empty rectal vault), Chagas disease (acquired loss of the plexus), and toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis or C. difficile colitis.
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: Hirschsprung disease; Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: toxic megacolon

GI-13-F.t: Explain Zenker diverticulum as a false pharyngoesophageal diverticulum above the cricopharyngeus from cricopharyngeal dysfunction, causing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis.
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: diverticulum (Zenker)

GI-13-F.t: Describe gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying from diabetic autonomic neuropathy, with early satiety and vomiting) and irritable bowel syndrome (recurrent pain linked to defecation and altered stool form without structural disease).
GI-13-F.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastroparesis; irritable bowel syndrome

GI-13-G.t: Explain appendicitis as luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) leading to distension, ischemia, and bacterial invasion, and trace pain from the periumbilical region (visceral) to McBurney point (parietal peritoneum) before perforation.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: appendicitis

GI-13-G.t: Describe Barrett esophagus as intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells replacing distal squamous epithelium after chronic reflux, and relate it to the dysplasia to adenocarcinoma sequence.

Explain how a low-fiber diet and high intraluminal pressure create false diverticula in the sigmoid colon where vasa recta penetrate the wall, and distinguish painless bleeding in diverticulosis from diverticulitis with left lower quadrant pain, fever, abscess, or fistula.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: diverticula, diverticulitis, diverticulosis

GI-13-G.t: Identify noninfectious causes of enteritis and colitis, including radiation, NSAIDs, and microscopic colitis (collagenous with a thick subepithelial collagen band, lymphocytic with excess intraepithelial lymphocytes) causing chronic watery diarrhea with normal-looking mucosa.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis; Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: microscopic colitis

GI-13-G.t: Compare gastric and duodenal ulcers by mechanism (H. pylori, NSAID loss of prostaglandin protection, Zollinger-Ellison), pain timing with meals, and malignancy risk, and predict hemorrhage or perforation with free air under the diaphragm.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastric ulcer; peptic ulcer; peptic ulcer perforation; duodenal ulcer

GI-13-G.t: Explain acute erosive gastritis and stress ulcers, including Curling ulcer after severe burns (hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia) and Cushing ulcer after brain injury (vagal stimulation raising acid), and NSAID and alcohol injury.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastritis

GI-13-G.t: Distinguish reflux esophagitis (basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae) from eosinophilic esophagitis (atopy, 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, rings and furrows, food impaction) and pill esophagitis (doxycycline, NSAIDs, potassium chloride).
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: esophagitis, pill esophagitis; Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: eosinophilic esophagitis

GI-13-G.t: Compare chronic H. pylori gastritis (antrum, intestinal metaplasia, risk of adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma) with autoimmune gastritis (body and fundus, parietal cell loss, achlorhydria, pernicious anemia).
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: gastritis

GI-13-G.t: Explain GERD from transient LES relaxation, low LES tone, and hiatal hernia (risks include obesity and pregnancy), and predict heartburn, chronic cough, hoarseness, and complications of stricture and Barrett esophagus.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: esophagitis, GERD; stricture and stenosis of esophagus

GI-13-G.t: Compare Crohn disease (mouth to anus, often terminal ileum, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, cobblestone mucosa) with ulcerative colitis (rectum extending proximally, continuous mucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps).
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: inflammatory bowel disease; granulomatous enteritis

GI-13-G.t: Predict complications of inflammatory bowel disease: fistulas, strictures, B12 and bile acid malabsorption, and oxalate stones in Crohn disease; toxic megacolon and primary sclerosing cholangitis in ulcerative colitis; colorectal cancer, erythema nodosum, uveitis, and arthritis in both.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: inflammatory bowel disease; toxic megacolon

GI-13-G.t: Distinguish Mallory-Weiss syndrome (mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction with hematemesis after retching) from Boerhaave syndrome (transmural esophageal rupture with chest pain, pneumomediastinum, and subcutaneous emphysema).
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: Mallory-Weiss syndrome; Gastrointestinal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: Boerhaave syndrome

GI-13-G.t: Distinguish anal fissure (posterior midline tear, painful bright red bleeding) from anorectal abscess and fistula (Crohn disease association), proctitis, and rectal prolapse.
GI-13-G.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: anal fissure, fistula, abscess, proctitis, rectal prolapse

GI-13-H.t: Describe esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula (the most common type), predicting polyhydramnios, drooling, choking and cyanosis with feeds, failure to pass a nasogastric tube, and air in the stomach, plus VACTERL associations.
GI-13-H.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Congenital disorders: esophageal atresia; tracheoesophageal fistula

GI-13-H.t: Distinguish esophageal webs (upper esophagus; Plummer-Vinson syndrome with iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and squamous cell carcinoma risk) from Schatzki rings (lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction, intermittent solid food dysphagia).
GI-13-H.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: stricture and stenosis of esophagus; dysphagia

GI-13-H.t: Describe Meckel diverticulum as a persistent vitelline duct forming a true diverticulum of the ileum, apply the rule of twos, and predict painless rectal bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa or obstruction from intussusception.

Explain infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, predicting nonbilious projectile vomiting at 2 to 6 weeks, a palpable olive-shaped mass, and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, with first-born males and macrolide exposure as risks.

Explain biliary atresia as progressive obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts, presenting in the first weeks of life with persistent conjugated jaundice, acholic stools, dark urine, and progression to cirrhosis.

Distinguish gastroschisis (defect usually right of the umbilicus, bowel not covered by peritoneum) from omphalocele (midline, covered by peritoneum and amnion, associated with trisomies and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome), and explain malrotation with Ladd bands.
GI-13-H.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: abdominal wall defects; Gastrointestinal: Congenital disorders: malrotation

GI-13-H.t: Explain cleft lip as failed fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes and cleft palate as failed fusion of the palatine shelves, and predict feeding difficulty.
GI-13-H.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Congenital disorders: cleft lip and palate

GI-13-I.t: Explain ascites in cirrhosis from portal hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, and splanchnic vasodilation with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation and sodium retention, and interpret a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more as portal hypertension.
GI-13-I.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the peritoneal cavity: ascites

GI-13-I.t: Distinguish spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (cirrhotic ascites, usually E. coli or Klebsiella, ascitic neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more) from secondary peritonitis (perforated viscus, polymicrobial, rigid abdomen).
GI-13-I.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: peritonitis, primary and secondary

GI-13-I.t: Explain how fibrous adhesions form after abdominal surgery or peritonitis and predict small bowel obstruction as their main complication.
GI-13-I.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: postsurgical adhesions

GI-13-J.t: Explain esophageal varices as dilated submucosal veins fed by the left gastric vein draining to the azygos system in portal hypertension, and predict painless massive hematemesis as a major cause of death in cirrhosis.
GI-13-J.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the liver and biliary system: portal hypertension, esophageal varices

GI-13-J.t: Distinguish internal hemorrhoids (above the pectinate line, painless bright red bleeding, prolapse) from external hemorrhoids (below the line, painful when thrombosed), and identify straining, constipation, pregnancy, and low-fiber diet as risks.
GI-13-J.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: hemorrhoids; rectal and anal hemorrhage

GI-13-J.t: Compare acute mesenteric ischemia (often an embolus from atrial fibrillation to the superior mesenteric artery, pain out of proportion to the exam, raised lactate) with chronic mesenteric ischemia (postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss) and ischemic colitis.
GI-13-J.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: mesenteric ischemia, ischemic bowel, ischemic colitis

GI-13-J.t: Describe angiodysplasia (dilated, tortuous submucosal vessels mostly in the cecum and right colon of older adults) as a cause of painless lower GI bleeding, and relate it to aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and end-stage kidney disease.
GI-13-J.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: angiodysplasia

GI-13-J.t: Explain necrotizing enterocolitis in premature infants as mucosal ischemia with bacterial invasion, predicting bloody stools, abdominal distension, and pneumatosis intestinalis on radiograph.
GI-13-J.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus: necrotizing enterocolitis

GI-13-K.t: Compare esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (upper and middle third; alcohol, tobacco, achalasia, caustic injury, Plummer-Vinson) with adenocarcinoma (distal third; GERD, Barrett esophagus, obesity), and predict progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids with weight loss.
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma

GI-13-K.t: Distinguish intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma (H. pylori, nitrosamines, atrophic gastritis, gland formation) from diffuse type (signet ring cells, linitis plastica, CDH1 loss), and identify metastatic signs (Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumor).

Identify gastric MALT lymphoma as an extranodal marginal zone B cell lymphoma driven by chronic H. pylori infection, and gastrointestinal stromal tumor as a KIT (CD117) mutant tumor of interstitial cells of Cajal, most often gastric.
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: stomach lymphoma, MALT lymphoma; GI stromal tumors

GI-13-K.t: Explain Zollinger-Ellison syndrome from a gastrin-secreting tumor of the duodenum or pancreas, predicting multiple or distal ulcers, diarrhea, steatorrhea from lipase inactivation by acid, a paradoxical gastrin rise after secretin, and MEN1 association.

Explain why carcinoid tumors of the small intestine cause carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, right-sided valve disease) mainly after liver metastasis, and identify raised urinary 5-HIAA as its marker.
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: GI carcinoid tumors; small intestine neoplasms

GI-13-K.t: Explain hepatocellular carcinoma risk factors (chronic HBV even without cirrhosis, HCV, alcohol, hemochromatosis, aflatoxin B1 with TP53 mutation) and findings (raised alpha-fetoprotein, hepatomegaly, hematogenous spread).

Identify metastases as the most common malignancy of the liver and peritoneum, and distinguish benign liver lesions: cavernous hemangioma (most common) and hepatocellular adenoma (oral contraceptive or anabolic steroid use, rupture risk).
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: metastatic neoplasms; peritoneal cancer

GI-13-K.t: Distinguish oral leukoplakia (white plaque that does not scrape off, may harbor dysplasia) from candidiasis (scrapes off) and hairy leukoplakia (EBV, lateral tongue, immunosuppression), and identify tobacco and alcohol as oral squamous cell carcinoma risks and HPV-16 as an oropharyngeal carcinoma risk.

Explain pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (KRAS mutation, smoking, chronic pancreatitis), predicting painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) in head tumors, migratory thrombophlebitis, weight loss, and raised CA 19-9.
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: pancreatic cancer; Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the pancreas: pancreatic duct obstruction

GI-13-K.t: Compare right-sided colon cancer (occult bleeding, iron deficiency anemia) with left-sided cancer (napkin-ring narrowing, change in bowel habit, obstruction), and identify risks (age, IBD, polyposis and Lynch syndromes) and CEA as a recurrence marker.
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: colon, rectal, and anal cancer

GI-13-K.t: Classify colonic polyps as hyperplastic, adenomatous (tubular, tubulovillous, villous, with malignant risk rising with size and villous component), sessile serrated, or hamartomatous (juvenile, Peutz-Jeghers).

Identify pleomorphic adenoma as the most common salivary tumor (usually parotid, mixed epithelial and stromal tissue, recurs if incompletely excised), Warthin tumor (smokers, lymphoid stroma), and mucoepidermoid carcinoma as the most common salivary malignancy.

Describe cholangiocarcinoma (primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis) and gallbladder adenocarcinoma (gallstones), predicting painless obstructive jaundice, and identify anal squamous cell carcinoma below the pectinate line as HPV-related.
GI-13-K.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Neoplasms: gallbladder cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, ampulla of Vater; anal cancer

GI-13-L.t: Explain pseudomembranous colitis: antibiotic disruption of colonic flora (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins), damage by C. difficile toxins A and B, yellow-white pseudomembranes, watery diarrhea, and toxic megacolon risk, diagnosed by stool toxin or toxin gene testing.
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: pseudomembranous colitis

GI-13-L.t: Distinguish causes of bloody enterocolitis (Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, EHEC, Entamoeba histolytica) and predict their complications: hemolytic uremic syndrome after EHEC O157:H7, Guillain-Barre syndrome after Campylobacter, and reactive arthritis.
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: enteric infections

GI-13-L.t: Distinguish infectious esophagitis in immunocompromised patients: Candida (white pseudomembranes, yeast and pseudohyphae), HSV-1 (punched-out ulcers, intranuclear inclusions), and CMV (linear ulcers, inclusions in endothelial and stromal cells).
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: infectious esophagitis (CMV, herpes)

GI-13-L.t: Match acute watery gastroenteritis to its setting: rotavirus (unvaccinated infants), norovirus (cruise ship and institutional outbreaks), ETEC (traveler's diarrhea), Vibrio cholerae (contaminated water, rice-water stool), and Bacillus cereus (reheated rice).
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: traveler's diarrhea; rotavirus enteritis

GI-13-L.t: Explain how plaque biofilm causes reversible gingivitis that can progress to periodontitis with loss of periodontal ligament and alveolar bone (Porphyromonas gingivalis), and relate acid from Streptococcus mutans to dental caries and tooth abscess.
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Disorders of the oral cavity, salivary glands, and esophagus: dental caries; abscessed tooth

GI-13-L.t: Describe oral thrush as Candida albicans overgrowth (budding yeast and pseudohyphae, white plaques that scrape off) and predict it in infants, inhaled corticosteroid or antibiotic use, diabetes, and HIV with low CD4 counts.
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: thrush

GI-13-L.t: Distinguish herpetic gingivostomatitis (primary HSV-1, fever with gum and lip vesicles), herpangina (coxsackie A, posterior pharyngeal vesicles), hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackie A16), and aphthous ulcers (Crohn disease, Behcet disease).
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: herpetic gingivostomatitis

GI-13-L.t: Interpret hepatitis B serology to identify acute infection (HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc), the window period (IgM anti-HBc alone), chronic infection (HBsAg over 6 months, IgG anti-HBc), resolved infection, and vaccination (anti-HBs alone).
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatitis B

GI-13-L.t: Predict outcomes of viral hepatitis: chronic HBV in most infected neonates but few adults, chronic HCV in most adults, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma with HBV or HCV, and HCV-related mixed cryoglobulinemia.
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatitis A, B, C, D, E

GI-13-L.t: Distinguish pyogenic liver abscess (biliary or portal spread, often E. coli or Klebsiella) from amebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica, anchovy paste fluid, travel history).
GI-13-L.usmle: Gastrointestinal: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: hepatic abscess
